source.title: A Theory of Inference Compute Scaling: Reasoning through Directed Stochastic Skill Search
source.authors: Austin R. Ellis-Mohr; A. Nayak; L. Varshney

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no evident truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops a theoretical and simulated account of downstream accuracy and compute allocation. Its simulations examine task-accuracy allocation paths and report task-dependent fitted scaling exponents and non-linear log-log trajectories, refining how stable power-law scaling should be understood. It does not directly measure held-out pretraining loss or reproduce the original loss-fitting experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper uses a cited pretraining-loss formula and discusses prior empirical scaling results, but those cited results are not its own. The model loss estimates in Appendix Table II are computed from that formula, not new held-out loss measurements. The paper's own relevant results are DS3 simulations, an accuracy-allocation simulation, and fitted optima over task difficulties. Empirical curves adapted from cited work are not treated as new model measurements.
record.test_reason: This is a theoretical paper (directed stochastic skill search, DS3). It takes the Hoffmann et al. loss fit, L = 1.69 + 406.4·N^-0.34 + 410.7·D^-0.28, as a given input. It maps that loss to skill success with a sigmoid and reports what its own model outputs: simulated accuracy curves and accuracy-maximising allocations of N, D and inference tokens Ω. None of its results measure held-out loss, extrapolation, loss-minimising allocation, shape effects or other modalities. The downstream-accuracy curves (Fig. 7) are DS3 simulations with rounded parameters chosen to align with cited Claude 3.7 and o1 AIME results. They reproduce a trend reported elsewhere and do not independently test whether real downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss. The allocation results (Fig. 8, 9, 16) optimise modeled accuracy under total or inference compute that includes inference tokens. That is a different objective from the loss-minimising compute-optimal split that V3 and V7 concern. So the study uses the scaling law as a tool rather than testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that DS3, which treats inference as stochastic traversal of a learned skill graph, unifies training and inference compute scaling. They say it theoretically recovers observed patterns: log-linear accuracy scaling, task-dependent preferred inference strategies, reasoning-elicited emergence, and BoN versus MV saturation. They also say jointly optimising model size, data and inference tokens is more efficient than Chinchilla-constrained or fixed-token allocations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a theoretical directed stochastic skill-search framework, sigmoid mapping from pretraining loss to skill proficiency, and simulated task-accuracy optimization rather than the original empirical held-out-loss fitting methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The inferred allocation and fitted scaling exponents vary with task difficulty and required skill count. The paper also notes sensitivity of its skill-directionality estimates to the assumed task distribution and lack of robustness analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: The DS3 simulation, with rounded parameters, reproduces linear accuracy gains with log training compute, log inference compute and log tokens used on AIME, aligned to cited Claude 3.7 Sonnet and o1 curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A skill-graph model of inference reproduces the log-linear downstream accuracy trends reported for reasoning models.

fits_no_version.finding: When modeled downstream accuracy is maximised under total compute 6ND + 2NIΩ, the optimal trajectories bend in log-log space. The optimal D/N rises above 20 with compute, and a Chinchilla-constrained path needs substantially more compute for equal accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When inference tokens are jointly optimised for downstream accuracy, the optimal pretraining allocation departs from the Chinchilla ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a fixed inference compute budget with unbounded data, fitted exponents for optimal model size (0.002–1.000, mean 0.367) and optimal inference tokens (0.245–1.000, mean 0.640) vary with task difficulty. One example task gives 0.28 and 0.72.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-compute-optimal splits between model size and inference tokens depend on task difficulty in the DS3 model.

record.peer_reviewed: Philosophical transactions. Series A, Mathematical, physical, and engineering sciences
record.problems: The relevant scaling results are primarily theoretical or simulated, with simplifying assumptions and no direct held-out pretraining-loss measurements. Some figures align models to publicly discussed or cited results rather than reporting new empirical runs. The paper itself notes that the directionality fitting is sensitive to the assumed task distribution and has not received thorough robustness analysis.
record.rows_left_out: No additional own results directly measuring the claim's held-out pretraining loss or its small-run extrapolation were reported. Results cited from other work, including empirical curves used as alignment references, were not extracted as this study's findings.

untested.parts: No own measurement of held-out pretraining loss against N, D or compute. The study uses the Hoffmann fit as an input.
No fit on small runs extrapolated to larger ones.

No loss-minimising allocation is measured. The framework's recovery of Chinchilla-style equal scaling is inherited from prior theory ([35]), and its new optima maximise modeled accuracy with inference costs included.
No variation of depth, width or other architecture at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes are only discussed. The pass@k fits are fitted to cited repeated-sampling data, not new scaling runs.
No real models are evaluated. The accuracy-versus-compute curves are DS3 simulations aligned to cited results.
No fitting choices, parameter counting, schedules or datasets are varied against real training runs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with V6 and V7 'supports' overstates this study. Every relevant result comes from the authors' own theoretical model fed with the Hoffmann loss law. The model is aligned by hand to cited empirical curves, so it is not an independent test. No verdicts are given. Fig. 14 (skill competence degrading away from κ≈20) is also a model output, from a framework the authors adjusted so that it reproduces Chinchilla behaviour. It is not evidence for V3.

versions.untested_parts: No own measurements of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
No test of whether loss laws fitted on small training runs predict much larger runs.

The optimization examples maximize modeled downstream accuracy and include inference compute; they do not test loss-minimizing parameter and training-token allocations or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann parameter-versus-data trends.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architectural choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes are discussed or cited, not tested with the paper's own results.

The paper models downstream accuracy from a loss-to-skill-proficiency mapping and reports simulated scaling trends; it does not establish empirical predictability across real models or tasks beyond the discussed AIME alignment.

The paper demonstrates task-dependent fitted exponents and non-linear modeled allocation curves, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting methods in experiments on real pretraining runs.

relation.reason: The Hoffmann loss fit is an input to the simulations. Their accuracy-maximizing training-plus-inference allocation differs from the loss-minimizing training allocation in V3.

tranche.reason: The study uses existing pretraining scaling laws and assumed skill mappings to derive its own inference and downstream-accuracy allocation results; it does not independently test the catalog versions.

source_check.notes: The numerical allocation results are hypothetical DS3 outputs; Claude/o1 curves are aligned to cited public results. No statements or verdict labels are listed in the check pack.
